articles.title: Hot or cold? Our research explores what works best after exercise
articles.author: Freya Bayne, Lecturer, Sport and Exercise Science, University of East London
paras: Ice baths have become one of the most popular recovery strategies in sport. They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym-goers to reduce soreness and recuperate more quickly after exercising.

It has often been claimed that ice baths help to reduce pain and repair the muscle damage that intense exercise can cause. Yet when we look at the evidence, it isn’t clear that ice baths really are the best way to recover post exercise.
In a recent study, my colleagues and I compared ice baths against heat-based recovery methods. What we found suggests recovery is far more complex than simply cooling things down.

Strenuous or unfamiliar exercise can cause damage to our muscle fibres. This is particularly the case after doing “eccentric exercises”, where muscles lengthen while generating force. Activities such as downhill running, descending the stairs or lowering a weight under control (while doing a barbell squat for instance) are all examples of eccentric exercise.

This exercise-induced muscle damage can leave your muscles feeling sore and weak. To repair the damage, the body triggers what’s known as an “inflammatory repair response”, where immune cells move into the muscle tissue to clear away damaged cellular material and stimulate regeneration.

Other molecules are also released to help coordinate repair. However, these molecules can also increase the sensitivity of pain receptors, which may further contribute to the muscle soreness that people experience up to 72 hours after an intense workout.
These responses are an important part of how the body repairs itself and becomes stronger.

We wanted to better understand what effect different recovery methods had on this repair process after a strenuous workout. So we recruited 40 healthy, physically active adults (31 men and nine women) and asked them to complete a specific exercise.

This involved repeatedly targeting the quadriceps – the large muscles at the front of the thigh – using a specialised machine that allowed us to carefully control the movement and measure muscle strength. This particular movement is known to cause temporary muscle damage and soreness – making it useful for studying how different recovery methods influence the body’s repair process.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery methods: cold-water immersion (in water that was 10°C), hot-water immersion (in water that was 42°C), hot air exposure (60°C, similar to a sauna) and “passive recovery” which involved sitting and doing nothing for 30 minutes. Each method was carried out immediately after the workout.

Over the following 72 hours, we monitored recovery by looking at several measures – including muscle strength, pain and soreness, alongside various biological markers linked to muscle damage, inflammation and cellular stress.
All participants showed the expected signs of exercise-induced muscle damage. Strength declined immediately after exercise and soreness increased.
But when we looked at the effects of the recovery techniques, we were surprised to find that none of them restored muscle strength significantly faster than the others.
If strength had been the only outcome measured, we might have concluded the recovery methods made little difference. But the physiological data told a different story.

Participants who completed hot-water immersion were shown to have higher levels of a substance called “heat shock protein 72” (HSP72) which acts as a cellular maintenance and protection system, supporting repair processes and protecting cells during periods of physiological stress. It’s widely believed that HSP72 plays an important role in recovery and adaptation following exercise.
The heat-based recovery methods were also associated with more favourable changes in biological markers linked to muscle damage and inflammation.
So our findings suggest that exposure to heat may be better at stimulating the biological processes involved in recovery.

Cold-water immersion was not shown to improve any of the recovery markers measured in the study. It also showed the slowest recovery, with strength returning to around 82% of pre-exercise levels after 72 hours, compared with 88-89% in the other groups.

But cold-water immersion appeared more effective at reducing perceptions of muscle soreness. This highlights how feeling recovered and actually being physiologically recovered are not always the same thing.

These findings should be interpreted with some caution, however. The study involved 40 healthy, physically active adults – with just ten participants in each intervention group. While the study was adjusted to detect moderate effects, the sample size wasn’t large enough to explore potential differences between men and women.
One of the most important lessons from our study is that recovery cannot be measured using a single outcome.
A person may feel less sore but may still have reduced muscle function. Also, important repair processes may be occurring inside the body without producing immediate improvements in performance.
This distinction may help explain why recovery research has produced mixed findings over the years. Different interventions may influence different aspects of recovery.

If your priority is reducing how sore you feel after a workout, cold-water immersion may be the most beneficial. But if your goal is to influence the biological processes that help your muscles to repair and adapt, heat-based recovery may be a better choice.
Our findings don’t suggest that ice baths are completely ineffective. Ice baths were still found to help people feel better.
What our study shows is that recovery is about far more than how you feel the next day. Sometimes the most important changes are happening beneath the surface.

articles.title: Blood sugar spikes: what actually works to manage them
articles.author: Gulshanara (Rumy) Begum, Senior Lecturer in Nutrition & Exercise Science, University of Westminster
paras: Blood sugar, also called blood glucose, rises after eating. Seeing that rise on a wearable monitor can make an ordinary meal look worrying. But a higher reading after lunch does not, by itself, mean that something has gone wrong.

The body uses glucose for energy. After a meal containing carbohydrate, glucose enters the bloodstream. In response, the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach, releases insulin. This hormone helps the body use glucose and store some for later.

For people with diabetes, managing blood glucose is essential. For people without diabetes, however, the benefits of tracking every rise and trying to flatten it are much less certain. A recent review found important gaps between claims about harmful “glucose spikes” and the available research.
So what can everyday habits do, and how much should we expect from them?

The type and amount of carbohydrate you eat affect how much your blood glucose rises after eating. Choosing fibre-rich foods, such as beans and wholegrains, is a good place to start. A review of clinical trials found that increasing fibre improved measures of blood glucose control in people with diabetes or prediabetes; where glucose levels are above the usual range but below the threshold for diabetes.

Another way of comparing foods that contain carbohydrates is the glycaemic index, or GI. It compares how much they raise blood glucose when portions containing the same amount of carbohydrate are eaten.

But GI tells only part of the story. It does not account for the portion you actually eat or the other foods on your plate. A food’s GI therefore cannot tell you exactly how your body will respond to a whole meal.

Other ingredients in a meal can change how high blood glucose rises and when it peaks. Adding fat, for example, may delay the rise without necessarily reducing the overall glucose response. A lower early peak does not, on its own, mean that a meal is healthier.

It may also matter which foods you eat first. A 2026 review of six small studies, involving 107 healthy adults, found that eating vegetables or protein-rich foods before carbohydrate-rich foods often reduced the rise in blood glucose shortly after eating.
However, these short studies, mainly involving young adults, do not show whether eating foods in a particular order prevents diabetes or improves long term health.
Movement can help your body use glucose
When muscles contract, they can take up glucose from the blood through processes that do not depend entirely on insulin.

Regular exercise has much more evidence behind it than individual post-meal movement strategies. A review of 100 randomised trials in adults with type 2 diabetes found that aerobic exercise, such as cycling, and resistance exercise, such as lifting weights, helped lower HbA1c. This is a measure of average blood glucose levels over the previous two to three months. Lower HbA1c levels generally indicate better long-term blood glucose control, which can help reduce the risk of diabetes-related complications.

Movement after eating may also help. A review of studies involving people with type 2 diabetes found that exercise after meals could reduce the subsequent glucose rise. The studies differed considerably, so they could not establish one ideal exercise routine or starting time.

Even a short walk may make a difference. In a small trial involving 12 healthy young adults, participants had a lower glucose response over two hours when they walked at a comfortable pace for ten minutes immediately after drinking a glucose solution than when they remained seated.

That is encouraging, but a glucose drink differs from dinner. The study cannot tell us exactly what a ten-minute walk will do after an ordinary meal for people of different ages and health backgrounds.

Researchers have also investigated seated “soleus push-ups”: repeated heel raises that work a muscle deep in the calf. In a 2025 pilot study, ten people with prediabetes had a lower glucose response while repeating the movement throughout a two-hour test involving a glucose drink test. This does not show that a few heel raises after lunch would have the same effect or improve glucose control over time.
Sleep matters too. Glucose regulation also depends on how effectively the body responds to insulin, known as insulin sensitivity.

A review combining results from randomised studies found that restricting sleep reduced insulin sensitivity in healthy adults. This supports paying attention to sleep alongside food and activity, although it does not show that an extra hour in bed will produce a particular glucose reading.

Wearable continuous glucose monitors use a small sensor beneath the skin to measure glucose in the fluid between cells and estimate glucose levels. They can be valuable in diabetes care, but current diagnostic guidance says there is insufficient evidence to use them to diagnose diabetes or prediabetes.

Diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests, usually with a second abnormal result to confirm the diagnosis unless it is already clear. A standard glucose-tolerance test uses a measured glucose drink, so its diagnostic thresholds cannot simply be applied to a reading after an ordinary meal.
People with diabetes need advice tailored to their medication and circumstances. Some treatments, including insulin, can cause dangerously low blood glucose, so lower readings are not always better.

For most people without diabetes, there is no established need to flatten every rise after eating. Focus instead on sustainable habits, such as including more fibre-rich foods, moving regularly and getting adequate sleep, rather than judging each meal by a glucose graph. If you repeatedly see unexpected readings or have symptoms that concern you, seek medical advice.

articles.title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
articles.author: Ziyad Al-Aly, Clinical Epidemiologist, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye.
I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION.

Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions.

The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.
Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.

NAION is an injury to the optic nerve, which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness.

These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.
How did the FDA identify the connection?

As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since 2021, when they were approved for obesity – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported an increased risk of the eye condition among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug.

To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the FDA first compiled data from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison.

Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.

In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of sentinel programs that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.

Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.
Is there other evidence of the risk?

Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION.

For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly 600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients.

That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk.

What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.

The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.

The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction.

But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of.
Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.

Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems. For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have risk factors for it, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.

articles.title: RFK Jr. loosens access to unapproved peptides: A health law scholar explains what consumers need to know
articles.author: Ana Santos Rutschman, Professor of Law, Villanova University
paras: Unregulated peptides for weight loss, muscle building, longevity and more are a roaring wellness fad – even though these substances have not been proved safe and effective and have not been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Until now, consumers were getting wellness peptides online through the so-called gray market, where companies rely on legal loopholes to sell them. Due to a push from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a vocal proponent of using peptides, an HHS policy on Oct. 29, 2026, will expand access to six peptides by allowing specialized pharmacies to make and sell them.
I am a health law professor who researches and teaches FDA law and policy. Consumers of peptides will soon have more options, but they should also be aware of the risks.
Drugs versus wellness products

Peptides are short chains of amino acids, which are building blocks for proteins. More than 7,000 peptides occur naturally in the human body. Some peptides – both natural and synthetic – have been developed as medicines, such as insulin and GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy.

Peptides that are commercialized as pharmaceutical drugs go through clinical trials and are approved by the FDA. But the slew of “wellness” peptides promoted by influencers and sold online or at wellness stores are not evaluated by any regulator.

American consumers have been able to buy wellness peptides online for over a decade. Until 2023 some of these peptides were sold at some specialized pharmacies as well. But that year the FDA restricted access to several wellness peptides due to unnamed “significant safety concerns,” forbidding specialized pharmacies from making and selling them. This did not prevent consumers from buying peptides online and at stores, however.

Since the early 2020s, the mainstreaming of wellness through the MAHA movement has driven up consumer interest in peptides. Access to nonpharmaceutical, unapproved products such as wellness peptides have long been a cornerstone of Kennedy’s personal philosophy and of the MAHA agenda.

Earlier this year, Kennedy pushed the FDA to review several peptides that the agency had restricted in 2023. Kennedy appointed eight new members to the committee that advises the FDA on these matters, all of whom had ties to businesses selling or promoting peptides. In July 2026 the committee voted 8-6 to expand access to six peptides: BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and TB-500.

The vote came after FDA scientists repeatedly told the committee that there was not enough information about the safety and efficacy of the peptides to justify letting compounding pharmacies sell them.

Some of these peptides are very popular, particularly on social media. For example, wellness influencers refer to the combination of BPC-157 and TB-500 as the “Wolverine stack,” after the Marvel comics superhero, often recommending it for building muscle mass and speeding up postworkout recovery. Kennedy has promoted these peptides in podcasts and as part of his Take Back Your Health tour.
The new policy allows small compounding pharmacies to sell these six peptides.

Compounding pharmacies are licensed to produce and sell a very small set of drugs that are not reviewed and approved by the FDA. Compounded drugs require a prescription and are meant for patients for whom there is no appropriate drug that is commercially available. For example, patients might need a drug in a strength or form that’s not specifically FDA-approved.

Normally the FDA does not encourage the sale of unstudied products. In this case, the agency is using a policy tool known as enforcement discretion to let these pharmacies know that there will be no legal consequences if they sell the six listed wellness peptides. This policy is often described as having an agency look the other way.
What is enforcement discretion?

When an agency employs enforcement discretion, it means that the law gives it authority to regulate an area but it chooses not to use that authority. This typically happens when the regulator thinks that a product poses very low risk to the public.
For example, during a recent shortage of some weight-loss drugs, the FDA used enforcement discretion to allow some compounding pharmacies to produce the drug to help ease the shortage.

However, if the FDA chooses not to enforce the law and the product poses risks to consumers, the consequences can be severe. The most notable case involved certain types of diagnostic tests, including tests for Lyme disease and breast and ovarian cancer. Several tests were on the market for a long time. For example, a company called Genomic Health started selling a breast cancer screening test in 2008. In 2011 scientists began questioning the accuracy of the test. In 2014 it was confirmed the test had provided false negatives to cancer patients.

The type of blood test that Elizabeth Holmes and her collaborators at Theranos claimed to have developed also belonged to the category of tests over which the FDA was exercising enforcement discretion. That was one of the reasons no one was monitoring Theranos properly, and that helped Holmes and her company hide their fraud for a long time.
What consumers should know

Kennedy and other proponents of peptides have said that it would be better for consumers to be able to buy them at compounding pharmacies, rather than online or at wellness stores, because these pharmacies are licensed to produce some medications that have not been approved by the FDA.

The new policy’s wording echos this sentiment, which implies that oversight by a pharmacist would somehow make these substances safer. However, compounding pharmacies have no obligation to test any ingredients they obtain from outside suppliers.

There is very little oversight of what is actually sold at these pharmacies. Federal law requires the FDA to evaluate drugs before they can be sold and to monitor their production. These requirements do not apply to compounded drugs.
The FDA’s own website notes that the lack of FDA regulation opens the door to “poor compounding practices” and that some compounded products can be unsafe or ineffective.
Under the new policy, there will be more places selling these wellness peptides, but there will still be no regulator checking their safety and efficacy.

More broadly, the FDA’s choice not to regulate peptides can have long-term effects for commercial research. FDA law incentivizes companies to do research on their products. But its new policy on peptides signals that the agency is not interested in having these products studied and evaluated. In my view, that may discourage studies exploring their use, including research that could uncover novel applications for them.

articles.title: What are biomarkers? A biologist explains how doctors measure your health – and how combining cells from different people can find new markers
articles.author: Michael F. Wells, Assistant Professor of Human Genetics, University of California, Los Angeles
paras: A family of five is exposed to the flu virus, but only two of them get sick. A lifelong chain-smoker lives 100 years, while a professional athlete in their prime dies of an unexpected heart attack. A drug fails a clinical trial due to harmful side effects in a subset of patients despite showing good results in others.
Could any of these scenarios have been predicted? The simple answer is not yet – but perhaps soon with the help of biomarkers.

A biomarker is anything measurable in the body that gives clinicians insight into someone’s current or future health. Biomarkers come in many forms and play a critical role in modern medicine by shedding light on the inner workings of the human body.
Many biomarkers are measured during routine procedures at the doctor’s office, including through blood tests and vital signs.

Physiological biomarkers such as heart rate and blood oxygen levels indicate how well your body is functioning. Cellular biomarkers such as white blood cell count provide useful information on the activity of your immune system. Genetic biomarkers are parts of your DNA that provide clues about your inherent risk of developing a particular disease or how likely you are to respond to a treatment.
There are still many more biomarkers to be discovered, and researchers are devising unique ways to identify a person’s risk of disease.
Discovering new biomarkers

The traditional way researchers identify biomarkers is by asking which biological features differ between two or more groups. This might look like comparing patients with a specific disease with healthy volunteers, people who respond to a drug with people who don’t, or the same group of people at two different points in time.

Many biomarker discoveries started with observations made in laboratories. For example, doctors use hemoglobin A1c levels in the blood to test for diabetes. The origins of this test date back to the 1960s, when scientists found abnormally high levels of a protein in the blood of diabetics. Repeated testing in the clinic over the next few decades confirmed the relationship between A1c levels and diabetes, culminating in the Food and Drug Administration approving the first A1c-based diabetes diagnostic test in 2013.

Other biomarkers that also started with observations made through basic research in the lab include screening tests for colorectal cancer, drug metabolism and inherited metabolic diseases in newborns.

Genetic biomarkers are typically found by scanning the genomes of thousands to even millions of people for genetic variants linked to a trait or disease. This approach is called a genomewide association study. This method has resulted in many important biomarkers that provide guidance on how to manage a patient’s risk of heart disease, age-related vision loss and liver disease.

One limitation of using the genomewide association study, though, is that it does not always provide information on which tissue or cell types may be relevant to the genetic variant. This lack of cellular information could be solved with cell cultures that allow researchers to study specific cell types under controlled conditions outside the body.
Human populations in a dish

In my work as a neuroscientist and geneticist, I take a different approach to finding biomarkers in the lab: I conduct genomewide association studies on human brain cells in a dish to understand how cells change when they encounter harmful exposures such as toxins and viruses.
Cells are the building blocks of all human tissues and organ systems. How sensitive they are to different environmental factors can greatly affect a person’s health and disease risk.

Thanks to revolutions in stem cell technologies, scientists are now able to model the effects of the environment on many different cell types – including brain cells that are nearly impossible to study in living people without causing irreversible damage to the brain. Instead, my colleagues and I obtain stem cells created from the blood or skin of human donors and convert them to brain cells for our experiments.

Most studies focus on how cells from only a handful of people respond to environmental stressors, mainly because it is quite difficult to conduct experiments at the population scale in a petri dish. To know whose cells are in a dish, researchers traditionally needed to handle and maintain cells from different people separately. This requirement adds considerable time, effort and cost for every new cell line included in the experimental design.

Because these issues limit the scale of experiments, studies aren’t able to capture the natural diversity of people and therefore cannot answer questions about why an exposure might make one person sick but have no effect on another.

My laboratory tackles this problem by pooling stem cell-derived brain cells from dozens to hundreds of people into the same culture dish – what my team calls a cell village. We use the genomes of these cells as natural barcodes to determine who donated each one. We then add different environmental perturbations to the village – such as pathogens, chemical pollutants and radiation – and measure how each person’s cells reacts.

Each cell might respond by turning on or off a set of genes, showing an increased or decreased propensity to die, or do nothing at all. Identifying which genes are linked to these particular responses can help explain why a person’s cells respond the way they do.
These genes are essentially biomarkers for the vulnerability of a specific cell type to an exposure.
An atlas of human vulnerability
While cell villages are relatively new, they have already helped researchers better understand what makes people different from each other.

For example, my team and I used cell villages to identify a biomarker that indicates a person may be particularly vulnerable to Zika virus infection. Zika is a pathogen spread by mosquitoes that can cause neurological disorders and microcephaly – small head size – in developing fetuses. Using stem cell-derived brain cells from 40 people, we found that not everyone was equally susceptible to infection. For some, fewer than 1% of their cells were infected by Zika virus; for others, it was greater than 99%.

Through additional cell village experiments, we discovered a genetic variant that regulates a powerful antiviral gene called IFITM3. In this case, the cells of a person with version A of this gene were more vulnerable to infection than the cells of a person with version B. Researchers have found links between this same genetic variant and COVID-19 and influenza A infection severity, suggesting it could be a genetic biomarker that can predict how certain people may respond to certain types of pathogens.

My team has also conducted similar work to identify genetic biomarkers for a person’s sensitivity to lead, a pervasive neurodevelopmental toxin. We are also using cell villages to find biomarkers for a person’s vulnerability to PFAS, also known as forever chemicals; measles virus infection; and stress hormones.
Our goal is to build what we call an atlas of human vulnerability: a catalog of genetic biomarkers to predict how each person might respond at the cellular level to a wide range of harmful exposures.
The cell village is only one of many emerging technologies that could usher in a new era of biomarker detection.

As DNA sequencing costs continue to drop, whole genome sequencing could become more routine in the clinic and potentially improve the ability to find links between genes and health outcomes that healthcare teams can intervene in.

Researchers are developing AI tools to survey medical imaging such as CT and MRI scans with the intention of finding new biomarkers for cancer progression that would have likely gone unnoticed by the human eye.

Cellphones and smartwatches may also be useful in efforts to discover new health-related biomarkers. For example, some studies have used these and other wearable devices to find behavioral biomarkers that predict major depressive episodes.

The goal now is to test how well these biomarkers work in the real world and make them widely available so that doctors everywhere can have as much information as possible about their patients when making life-changing decisions.

articles.title: How babies are born knowing the difference between day and night
articles.author: Timothy Hearn, Lecturer, University of Cambridge; Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Before a baby sees its first sunrise, it is already receiving signals about day and night. Melatonin, a hormone released mainly at night, can pass from the mother through the placenta. The placenta supplies the developing foetus with oxygen and nutrients.

This may help explain interest in a Japanese study of 31,528 mothers and children. It found a link between working night shifts during pregnancy and possible developmental difficulties in children at age four. But it could not show that night work caused those difficulties.

Researchers compared women who did not work night shifts, women who stopped between two pregnancy surveys, and women who reported night shifts at both surveys. Working just one night shift a month counted as night work. The study did not examine whether more frequent shifts carried greater risks.

Children whose mothers reported night shifts at both stages had a 29% to 34% higher relative risk of being flagged for possible difficulties with communication, fine motor skills (such as picking up small objects) or social skills, compared with children whose mothers did not work nights.
That does not mean a third of these children had difficulties. Across all groups, about 13% of children were flagged for a possible difficulty in at least one area.
Parents answered questions about their children’s abilities. These were screening checks, not medical diagnoses. A flagged result means a child might need further assessment.
The study had limitations. Researchers did not know exactly how many nights the women worked, how demanding their jobs were or why some stopped working nights.

Researchers also looked at sleep duration. The link between night work and developmental screening results appeared stronger among women who reported sleeping at least ten hours. But only 80 women both continued working nights and reported that much sleep. This finding is uncertain and does not show that sleeping longer is harmful.
The study also cannot tell us whether stopping night shifts would reduce any risk.
How babies learn about day and night

One possible explanation involves the body’s internal clock. This controls daily patterns in sleep, hormones and other processes. Before birth, the internal clock is still developing, so signals from the mother may help tell day from night.

Night work can disturb this timing. Even when someone gets enough sleep, sleeping during the day and staying awake at night can put their routine out of step with their body clock. Light and meal times can affect it too.

Animal research offers clues about how these signals reach a foetus in the womb. In a 2025 rat study, researchers found that substances from the mother’s food rose and fell throughout the day in an area of the unborn rat’s brain that would later help control its body clock. This happened before the clock was fully working.
In a 2026 mouse study, researchers gave pregnant mice a stress-related hormone at different times of day. The timing changed daily rhythms in their developing offspring and the placenta.

These studies suggest that food-related substances and hormones may help pass information about time from mother to foetus. But they do not show whether this explains the Japanese findings or happens in the same way in humans.
What early light exposure can tell us
Other mouse studies have tested whether the amount of daylight during early life affects body clocks later on.

Mice raised under long, summer-like days developed different patterns of activity in their brain clocks from mice raised under short, winter-like days. Some differences remained after the lighting changed.

Another study exposed mice to different day lengths from pregnancy until weaning. Even after they were put on the same light and dark schedule, mice raised under longer days spent more time asleep during daylight hours.

These experiments suggest that early light patterns can have lasting effects on mice. But seasonal changes in daylight are very different from working night shifts, and the findings cannot tell us whether human babies are affected in the same way.

Timing signals may also continue after birth. Breast milk contains melatonin, and its levels change through the day. In a small 2026 trial involving 60 premature babies, those given expressed milk at the same time of day it had been collected spent longer in quiet sleep by the time they left hospital. The researchers did not look at longer-term development.

Scientists are still learning how babies receive signals about day and night. The Japanese study raises useful questions about supporting pregnant night workers, including whether more flexible working hours could help. But it cannot establish that disrupted body clocks caused developmental difficulties, and it gives parents no reason to fear that an occasional sleepless night will harm their child.

articles.title: Tanning and homemade sunscreen trends overlook what sunlight does to your skin
articles.author: Charareh Pourzand, Reader, Department of Pharmacy and Pharmacology, University of Bath
paras: After more than 30 years studying how sunlight damages skin, I find the renewed enthusiasm for deliberate tanning worrying. On social media, a trend known as “tanmaxxing” encourages people to pursue increasingly deep tans, sometimes by using UV-index forecasts to seek out the strongest sunlight and avoiding sunscreen altogether.
In the laboratory, the damage caused by ultraviolet radiation is measurable. Yet online discussions can make avoiding sunscreen sound like the healthier choice.

Questions about sunscreen ingredients deserve serious answers. So do questions about vitamin D. But answering them means looking at research, including its limitations, rather than assuming that something described as “natural” must be safe.

Sunlight reaching the Earth contains two types of ultraviolet radiation: UVA and UVB. UVB is responsible for most sunburn and can directly damage DNA, the genetic instructions inside cells. UVA penetrates more deeply into skin and contributes to premature ageing. Both can contribute to skin cancer. Research on sunscreen and skin damage supports protection against both.
A tan may look reassuring, particularly if you have been told to develop a “base tan” before a holiday. But the colour does not tell you that your skin is adequately protected.

In experiments on human skin, researchers found that tans produced by UVA offered no meaningful protection against subsequent DNA damage. UVB-induced tans provided only modest protection. Deliberately exposing skin to UV to prepare it for more exposure therefore brings damage of its own.

Sunbeds add another source of exposure. A systematic review and meta-analysis linked indoor tanning with increased risks of melanoma and other skin cancers. Starting young and using sunbeds frequently were associated with greater risks.
That does not mean everyone who used a sunbed as a teenager will develop cancer. Increased risk is not a prediction of a person’s future but it does mean avoiding further exposure is worthwhile.

Sunscreen has evidence behind it, although no product offers complete protection. In the long-term follow up of an Australian randomised trial, researchers recorded fewer melanomas among people assigned to daily sunscreen use than among those who used it at their discretion. The total number of cases was small, so the estimate was uncertain, but the findings supported a protective effect.

Concerns about ingredients still need investigation. A clinical trial found that some sunscreen ingredients could enter the bloodstream under intensive application conditions. Detecting absorption did not establish that those ingredients caused harm. The researchers explicitly said their findings were not a reason to stop using sunscreen.

Making your own product introduces a different problem: you cannot judge its protection by its appearance or ingredients list. In a laboratory study of 15 internet sunscreen recipes, none provided adequate protection. Three contained no UV filters; the remaining preparations had measured sun protection factors (a measure of how well sunscreen protects skin against UVB radiation) below six.
Adding zinc oxide to a mixture of oils does not establish a reliable SPF. The finished formulation needs testing, including how evenly it protects the skin.

The issues around Vitamin D require a more nuanced answer than either side of the sunscreen debate sometimes offers. Skin uses UVB to make vitamin D, which has important functions in the body, from maintaining strong bones to supporting immune function. This means that reducing UVB exposure through the use of sunscreen can affect production.

A 2019 holiday study found that properly applied SPF15 sunscreen allowed vitamin D levels to rise while preventing sunburn. However, a 2025 Australian randomised trial found that routine SPF50+ use over about a year resulted in lower vitamin D levels than discretionary sunscreen use. These studies examined different products and circumstances.

The practical response is to address vitamin D without deliberately damaging skin. UK advice is that adults should consider a daily 10-microgram supplement during autumn and winter. Some people, including those with dark skin or little sun exposure, should consider supplementation throughout the year.

My own research examines damage that happens inside skin cells after UVA exposure. In research using human skin cells, my colleagues and I showed that UVA could release iron from ferritin, a protein that stores it. This available iron can help drive chemical reactions that damage cellular components. Sun exposure is certainly no treatment for iron deficiency.

This has led to research on antioxidants and compounds that bind iron, potentially limiting that damage. The aim is to improve skin protection. Laboratory findings do not, however, establish that any cream containing an antioxidant will prevent skin cancer, or compensate for inadequate sunscreen application.

For now, the practical priorities are well established. NHS guidance recommends SPF30 or higher with at least four-star UVA protection. A circled UVA logo indicates that a product meets the relevant European UVA standard.

Apply sunscreen generously to exposed skin. Adults covering their whole body need roughly six to eight teaspoons. Reapply every two hours while exposed, and after swimming or towel drying. Use clothing and shade alongside sunscreen, particularly around midday.

A sunscreen you can afford and comfortably use in sufficient quantities is more useful than an expensive product applied sparingly. Enjoying time outdoors and protecting your skin are perfectly compatible; a tan is not a requirement for either.

articles.title: The collagen craze promises younger-looking skin, but the evidence is less convincing
articles.author: Katie Edwards, Commissioning Editor, Health + Medicine and Host of Strange Health podcast, The Conversation
paras: Collagen marshmallows are now a thing. So are collagen crisps. If neither appeals, you can stir collagen powder into your morning coffee.

Social media is full of products promising to replenish the collagen we lose as we age. The claims extend beyond firmer skin and fewer wrinkles to healthier joints and improved gut health. Some supplements cost £40 or more per month.
But what happens to collagen when we eat it? And can these products persuade our bodies to make more?

In this episode of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast investigating unusual health and wellness trends, I explore the collagen boom with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.
Our guest is Joan Chang, a collagen researcher and senior lecturer at the University of Manchester, who explains why the answer is more complicated than a scoop of powder.
Can collagen supplements deliver what they promise?

Collagen is the body’s most abundant protein. It provides the structural framework for our skin and tendons, among other tissues. But it isn’t one substance doing one job. Scientists have identified at least 28 types, with different structures and functions.
As we get older, collagen production and maintenance change. That has helped create a market for products promising to replace what we’re losing.

Chang explains why consuming collagen doesn’t mean it will be delivered intact to your face or knees. The digestive system breaks it down into smaller components, which the body can use in different ways.

Some clinical trials suggest benefits for skin hydration or elasticity, but the evidence is contested. A 2025 review of 23 trials found that apparent improvements disappeared when researchers looked only at higher-quality studies or those without pharmaceutical-industry funding.

And what about applying collagen directly to your face? Chang explains why large collagen molecules generally cannot pass through intact skin, leaving many collagen creams functioning mainly as moisturisers.
From salmon DNA to artificial corneas

The episode also ventures into the stranger corners of the beauty industry, including PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide, if you fancy trying to pronounce it), an ingredient often derived from salmon or trout DNA that’s being marketed as the latest way to boost collagen and rejuvenate skin.
Baumgarddt examines the evidence, including an important distinction between using a substance in wound healing and expecting a serum to rejuvenate healthy skin.

We also look at microneedling, where tiny needles deliberately puncture the skin to stimulate repair. Professional treatments may improve scarring, but home attempts carry risks, including infection and further scarring.

Looking to the future, some of collagen’s most remarkable applications are in medicine. Researchers have used its structural properties to develop wound dressings and experimental corneal implants designed to restore sight.
Listen to the episode for a closer look at what collagen can do, which claims deserve scrutiny and whether your next skincare purchase really needs to involve fish DNA.

articles.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
articles.author: Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia
paras: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages, which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease.

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test, by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.
But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.
As a physician who studies early cancer detection, and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group, I have been following this test’s development with interest.

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.

On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test.

But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.
Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.
What is the Galleri test? How does it work?

Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests. These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.

The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.

Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result.
What are the strengths of the Galleri test?

The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers, including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S, such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer.

Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.
In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range.

This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV, which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens, meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.

For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.

The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients. Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body.
What are the limitations of the Galleri test?
Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings.

For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases. Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.

In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening, meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages, so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result.

Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so. In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this.

There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.
Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.
What did the FDA’s panel recommend?
The FDA advisory panel took three votes. While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.

First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.

These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure, but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.

Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test.

This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer.

Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low?

While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.
The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.
Should you get the Galleri test or not?

If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.

First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a separate coverage determination process, and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is currently US$949.

It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.

What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with currently recommended cancer screening tests for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.

articles.title: Why do farts smell so bad? A microbiologist explains the odors brewing in your gut
articles.author: Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, New York, New York
A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. All together, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.
So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?
Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.
Your gut’s source of grody gases
The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.
However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness book of world records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mis-hears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.
So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

articles.title: For veterans with mild traumatic brain injury, a restaurant or other noisy environment can feel like a battlefield
articles.author: Jeffrey Hebert, Associate Professor of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: Imagine sitting down with your family at a restaurant. Conversations at your table overlap with those of patrons seated nearby. Utensils clink on plates. Waitstaff weave between tables. Music plays overhead.

Many people might find the bustle of such a scene a bit annoying. However, for veterans with chronic mild traumatic brain injury, or TBI, also referred to as concussion, busy environments like this are frequently intolerable. What should be an enjoyable social event soon escalates to internal mayhem. They find their attention stretched beyond capacity. Tension and irritability grow. The impulse to flee or fight becomes paramount.
Veterans who have chronic mild TBI and have described these experiences to me often ask: “Why does this keep happening?”

I am a clinical neuroscientist providing treatment and rehabilitation at an institute in Colorado for military service members and veterans who have experienced concussions. Some of the most common challenges I see in my patients are irritability and cognitive problems. With this knowledge, my scientific efforts focus on discovering the causes of these persistent symptoms.

My colleagues’ and my research is revealing that these challenges may largely be due to the injured brain being flooded by sensory information that overwhelms its processing capacity. This may explain why even a mild brain injury can interfere with military service members’ transition to civilian life.

Mild TBIs are among the most common injuries that military service members experience and are considered the signature injury of recent wars and ongoing conflicts. Since 2000, more than 500,000 military service members have experienced a TBI, according to the Defense Health Agency. More than four out of five of these injuries are classified as “mild”.

Many people appear to recover quickly from these injuries, within weeks or a couple of months, but for a considerable number of others, symptoms and measurable brain changes persist years or even decades later.

Military service members and veterans often experience post-traumatic stress and mild TBI together. Studies have linked the two conditions collectively to changes in behavior, cognitive complaints and negative impact on their spousal relationship and family satisfaction and functioning.

Addressing these issues solely through a psychological lens has its limits, since many of these problems happen while the veteran is trying to function in environments that can lead to sensory overload.
A sensory bottleneck in the injured brain

Throughout the day, the human brain is tasked with managing multiple sensory inputs. It is constantly working to pay attention to what’s most relevant while filtering out whatever might distract it from functioning properly.
But for the injured brain, the filtering process often malfunctions. This can create a bottleneck of sensory information, which stresses the brain’s processing capacity.

In a 2026 study of military veterans, my colleagues and I found that in people with chronic mild TBI, symptoms of irritability were intertwined with post-traumatic stress symptoms and sensory problems such as pain and difficulties processing speech in noisy environments.

In other words, veterans with chronic mild TBI are simultaneously trying to manage ongoing pain, distinguish speech from competing sounds, maintain attention and regulate emotional responses. That may be why busy environments are so burdensome for them: These demands deplete the brain’s bandwidth, pushing it beyond its threshold.
The consequences of visual challenges

In another recent study, my research team and I found that veterans with chronic mild traumatic brain injury experience difficulties such as quick eye movements and challenges with cognition, including attention, impulsivity and verbal fluency.

Crowded restaurants, grocery stores, airports and family gatherings contain a great deal of visual motion. One of the vision tests in the study is similar to the problem our veterans face in these real-world environments. In these environments, the inability to stop getting distracted by movement in their vision, often referred to as the “squirrel” moment, is a consistent complaint. In our study, we found that the difficulty suppressing that impulse is a problem for veterans with chronic mild TBI and is directly associated with their ongoing difficulties in attention, impulsivity and processing speed.

Increased visual stimulation creates more cognitive load, consuming resources the brain needs to manage other demands. For example, the injured brain also needs to simultaneously manage psychological stress, pain and sound that further deplete the brain’s reserves.
Everyone is equipped with a limited amount of brain and cognitive reserves.

Healthier brains tend to have a larger reserve that withstands onslaughts of sensory stimuli and challenges to emotional and cognitive control. In contrast, the injured brain has a limited reserve or threshold, leading to irritability, poor attention and impulsivity, making socializing with family and friends intolerable.

These limitations aren’t simply an annoyance or added challenge; they test the brain’s ability to continuously, efficiently and effectively process and respond to a world filled with constant incoming sensory data.
For veterans living with the long-term effects of mild TBI, understanding this paradox can often be one of the most important steps toward seeking the most appropriate care.

articles.title: Back pain: how your doctor’s words could influence your recovery
articles.author: Dave Newell, Professor of Integrated Musculoskeletal Care and Head of the Centre of Pain and Active Inference Research, Health Sciences University
paras: Jenny’s back pain usually settles within a few weeks. This time, 12 weeks have passed and it still intrudes on her life. Getting dressed hurts. Sitting through work is difficult. And something else is becoming harder to ignore: worry.
Why hasn’t it gone away? Is something seriously wrong? Will it ever get better?
Social media offers plenty of alarming possibilities. Jenny starts monitoring every twinge. Each painful movement seems to confirm that something must be wrong.

Jenny is fictional, but her experience may be familiar. When she consults her doctor, she might expect relief from exercise, medication or hands-on treatment. Could the consultation itself also influence her pain?

Imagine two versions of Jenny’s appointment. In one, the doctor interrupts her and describes her back as “worn out”. Jenny leaves with exercises, but also with a disturbing picture of a fragile spine.

In the other, the doctor listens, explores her concerns and examines her carefully. Finding no signs suggesting a serious underlying cause, they explain what they have assessed, acknowledge how disabling her pain is and discuss a manageable plan.
Both appointments might include the same exercises, but Jenny may leave with different expectations about her back.
Researchers call these surrounding influences “contextual factors”. They include expectations, past experiences, the doctor’s communication and the care setting.

Studies suggest these factors are linked to treatment outcomes. In one study involving 182 people with longstanding back pain, a stronger relationship with their physiotherapist early in treatment was associated with better outcomes after eight weeks.

Another UK study involving 960 patients receiving physiotherapy, osteopathy or acupuncture found that the relationship between patient and practitioner was among the strongest predictors of reduced disability. Agreement about treatment goals and how to achieve them was particularly important.
These observational studies cannot establish that the relationship caused improvement, but they suggest that what happens during a consultation deserves attention.
How words can influence pain
If Jenny’s pain is in her back, how could someone’s manner or explanation influence it?
Pain is not a straightforward measure of damage: its intensity does not always match the extent of tissue injury.

One possible explanation comes from predictive processing theories. These suggest that the nervous system interprets signals from the body alongside previous experiences, expectations and present circumstances.

For Jenny, pain that once meant “another episode that will settle” may now mean “something dangerous that nobody has identified”. This change in expectation could contribute to her pain feeling more threatening.
This is one possible explanation of persistent pain. It does not mean Jenny has consciously caused her symptoms.

There is experimental evidence that expectations can influence pain. In one study, healthy volunteers received a powerful opioid painkiller while experiencing painful heat. Positive expectations roughly doubled the drug’s pain-relieving effect, while negative expectations abolished it.
The drug was still being delivered, but participants received different information about it. Brain scans also showed changes in activity in regions involved in processing pain.

This suggests that expectations can influence pain through measurable biological processes. However, findings from short laboratory experiments cannot tell us exactly how much a particular consultation will affect someone with longstanding back pain.
Giving reassurance something to stand on
Simply saying “there’s nothing wrong” is unlikely to address Jenny’s experience. Something plainly is wrong: she hurts, cannot do what she normally does and wants to understand why.
A useful explanation would acknowledge this while distinguishing pain from evidence of serious disease. It would explain the assessment and give Jenny opportunities to ask questions.
The doctor might also ask what she fears. Perhaps her main worry is that bending will damage her spine. Exercises alone may leave that concern untouched.

A theory called “active inference” offers another way to understand this. It proposes that expectations influence what people do, while their actions provide new information that can change those expectations.

In a 2026 paper applying this approach to pain affecting muscles and joints, researchers suggest that movement, communication and other aspects of care may help patients develop different expectations about their bodies.

If Jenny expects bending to cause damage, she may avoid it. With appropriate clinical guidance, gradually exploring that movement could help her discover that her back is more capable than she feared.

This theory may help explain how care works, but researchers have not shown that applying it improves outcomes beyond existing treatments. Treatments also have specific effects that cannot be explained by context alone.

A reassuring consultation cannot replace appropriate assessment or effective treatment, repair an injury or guarantee recovery. Nor does the importance of context justify offering unproven treatments simply because they are delivered with a good bedside manner.
Patients should never be blamed for continuing pain or told they need to think positively.

For doctor, the practical message is to combine careful assessment and evidence-based treatment with explanations that inform without creating unnecessary alarm. UK clinical guidance supports shared decisions, advice about remaining active and individually appropriate treatment for lower back pain.
Patients can reasonably ask what might be causing their pain, whether there are signs of anything serious and what activities they can safely continue.

Jenny needs her pain taken seriously, her concerns heard and a credible way forward. The way that care is offered may help shape what happens next, including her confidence in moving and managing pain.
